title: Global Liquidity Peaks: The More Aggressively a Company Spent on AI in H1, the Sooner It Gets Discounted
dek: A rising capital market requires new money to keep buying in. Global liquidity is already showing signs of peaking, and the companies that were most aggressive on AI in the first half are shifting from being rewarded to being discounted.
why: It puts US AI capex, Hong Kong IPOs and household balance sheets on the same funding chain — a macro framework that does not treat AI as a panacea.
who: For investors watching both US AI stocks and China/Hong Kong asset allocation, and for primary-market practitioners judging where and when hot money will flow in 2025.
skip: The case-by-case discussion of Hong Kong IPOs can be skipped; the main thread starts at 8:11 with Nvidia's liquidity experiment.

points.h: A low IPO break rate is not a good signal
points.body: Do not read Hong Kong's low first-day break rate as a sign of market strength. In the first half of this year the break rate was only in the teens, far below the roughly fifty-fifty level that a market-based mechanism would produce. That means the main participants in these IPOs are short-term speculative arbitrage funds, not long-term investors. Recently the supply of new listings has shrunk and IPO-related funds have blown up, yet the two most recent listings still broke issue, showing that temporary supply-side controls have not solved the underlying problem: Hong Kong also faces peak liquidity.

points.h: The more aggressive on AI, the sooner punished
points.body: Market attitude reversed within a single quarter. Before Q1, the capital market rewarded aggression: the louder the AI CapEx, the higher the valuation. By late July, when half-year reports were disclosed en masse, any large internet company that had made aggressive capex in the first half — especially those that burned through free cash flow — was discounted, and even Google was not exempt. Q2 was precisely the quarter of maximum FOMO across the entire supply chain, with everyone rushing to spend before prices rose, and inventories still propping up gross margins. By Q3, inventories are depleted and the impact of price increases returns, so the negative factors will show up together.

points.h: Nvidia is closer to Cisco in 2000
points.body: Nvidia's earnings look good, but its cash flow is changing. Before the dot-com bubble burst in 2000, Cisco rolled out 'lease-to-buy' to help customers finance purchases, pulling future revenue forward into current sales. Nvidia is now also pushing lease-to-buy. In its financials, free cash flow halved quarter-on-quarter, and accounts receivable are far above historical levels — speculated to be partly related to the credit enhancement and collection structure that lease-to-buy brings. So Nvidia may have reached a stage where it needs more aggressive financial engineering to sustain capital-market expectations, similar to Cisco's situation back then.

points.h: Primary-market money comes from bullets fired three years ago
points.body: The answer lies in fund-raising timing. The money that will be deployed heavily into AI and robotics from H2 2025 to H1 2026 mainly comes from funds raised at the market peak in 2020-2022; they barely invested in 2023-2025, until they saw state capital placing bets when no one dared and earning the most — the stories of ChangXin and ChangCun, two large models, and two large chips stimulated market-based capital. The mindset is: copy the state capital's homework. So this is not a rational long-term incremental wave, but more like a delayed emotional release.

points.h: Property policy removes households from the financing chain
points.body: The key to recent real estate policy is not bailing out developers, but pulling households out of the old financing loop. In the past, buying a pre-sale home meant the household played the role of financing target in the investment-driven chain: pay first, receive later. The policy pushes the chain toward marketization, so buyers get completed homes and only bear the consumer role, with risk reset back to developers and financing institutions. The policy was introduced when home prices were near the bottom to first stabilize the denominator on the asset side, avoiding panic from dismantling the chain during a downturn. Japan after the 1990s and China's coal and mining consolidation followed similar paths.

points.h: A slow bull is not a slogan, it is chip structure
points.body: A slow bull does not rely on slogans; it relies on layering market chips by duration. At the bottom are low-valuation, high-dividend blue chips held by insurers as long money that rarely trades. Above that are mutual funds and index funds, performing a quasi-stabilizing function. Central Huijin and China Securities Finance adjust the index at a higher layer. At the top are retail investors, private funds and active managers. New insurance regulations require liabilities and assets to match in term, yield and liquidity, effectively ensuring long money invests long, medium money medium, and short money short — no using ordinary people's short money to invest in ten-year illiquid assets.

points.h: Crises get bigger with each rescue, bubbles at least one and a half
points.body: After the US dollar left gold in 1971, global central banks became increasingly accustomed to printing money to directly intervene in crises, acting faster each time. The quantitative easing after 2008 should have been cleared during a rate-hiking cycle, but was interrupted by political intervention, and then came the pandemic in 2020, so a larger wave of easing was layered on top of a bubble that had not yet dissipated — today we have accumulated at least one and a half bubbles. Central bank governors have learned to print more money immediately when a crisis appears, and the endogenous result is simultaneous increases in inflation, financial asset prices and wealth inequality. As long as bubbles are not allowed to clear, the world may face long-term stagflation in some form.

quotes.text: The reason I say it feels a bit precarious is that today the whole world has a bit of a liquidity peak problem.
In the capital market, whoever spends aggressively is seen as impressive, and then when half-year reports come out, it becomes whoever is aggressive gets punished.
Perhaps Nvidia has also reached a point where it needs lease-to-buy to drive revenue growth and meet capital market expectations.
Everyone sees that you can pull off this story this way, so I can definitely pull it off this way too — psychologically that's roughly it.
The so-called slow bull we always talk about is not because it is inherently slow and bullish; on the basis of a slow bull, you first have to build a chip structure.
When the bubble piled up last time had not yet dissipated, a bigger one was added — and added without hesitation.
